title: Certainty and the Arbitrary
summary: The arbitrary as neither true nor false, and certainty as contextual.

lessons.title: A claim with nothing behind it
lessons.objective: Recognize an arbitrary assertion as a claim offered with no evidence and no tie to the facts you know.

exercises.prompt: What makes an assertion arbitrary?

choices.text: It is offered with no evidence connecting it to the facts
It is unusual, even though the evidence is strong
It is difficult to prove, but some evidence supports it
It was learned only recently

feedback.note: Arbitrary means unsupported. Novelty or difficulty is not the test; the absence of evidence is.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is arbitrary?

choices.text: An unseen force rearranges your books at night, and nothing you know gives a reason to think so
The street is wet, so rain is one candidate you can check
Two added to two is four, on the rules of arithmetic you already use
The cup is on the table, because you see it there

feedback.note: The unseen force is asserted with no link to observation or to anything already known. The other claims rest on perception, calculation, or a checkable clue.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to why it is, or is not, arbitrary.

pairs.left: A number no one can ever relate to any fact
pairs.right: Arbitrary: no evidence ties it to reality

pairs.left: The stove is hot because you burned your hand
pairs.right: Not arbitrary: a percept supports it

pairs.left: A hypothesis you can test against known measurements
pairs.right: Not arbitrary: it is tied to evidence you can check

feedback.note: A claim leaves the arbitrary when some evidence, perceptual or conceptual, connects it to what is.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition used in this lesson.

parts.text: An arbitrary assertion is offered with no

feedback.note: Without evidence, the assertion does not yet belong in thinking about what is true.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the mark of the arbitrary.

feedback.note: The mark is missing evidence, not unpopularity and not a finished proof of something else.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, I simply prefer to assert it. What is the status of that assertion?

choices.text: Arbitrary, because a preference is not evidence
True, because sincerity counts as proof
Automatically false, because it was said aloud
Certain, because no one contradicted it yet

feedback.note: Wanting a claim, or saying it with confidence, does not connect it to the facts.

exercises.prompt: Which addition would stop a claim from being arbitrary?

choices.text: Evidence that relates the claim to something already known
Repeating the claim more often
Giving the claim a special name
Warning that doubters will be sorry

feedback.note: Only a cognitive link to reality removes the arbitrary. Volume, labels, and threats do not.

exercises.prompt: Fill the missing standard.

parts.text: the claim, treat it as arbitrary.

feedback.note: Support means a reason drawn from what you know, not a feeling about the claim.

exercises.prompt: Match the offering to its cognitive standing.

pairs.left: Assertion with no reason at all
pairs.right: Arbitrary
Tied to evidence
Tied to evidence

feedback.note: Evidence can be a percept or a conclusion already based on facts. A bare assertion has neither.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule for spotting the arbitrary.

feedback.note: Lack of a tie to the facts is the definition used here, not a reason to believe the claim.

lessons.title: Neither true nor false
lessons.objective: Treat the arbitrary as cognitively empty: it is neither true nor false, so it is set aside instead of weighed as a candidate.

exercises.prompt: What truth-value does an arbitrary claim have?

choices.text: Neither true nor false
True until someone disproves it
False because it lacks evidence
Both true and false at once

feedback.note: With no evidence, the claim has not entered the realm of true or false. Lack of evidence does not by itself prove the opposite.

exercises.prompt: How should you handle an arbitrary claim in thinking?

choices.text: Set it aside; it is not a candidate to weigh
Adopt it, since it might turn out true
Count it as half true
Assert the opposite with equal force and no evidence

feedback.note: The proper response is dismissal from cognition, not belief and not an equally empty denial.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the response it calls for.

pairs.right: Set aside; it is neither true nor false
Judge it false

pairs.left: Claim that the evidence fully supports
pairs.right: Judge it true

feedback.note: True and false apply once a claim has a relation to evidence. The arbitrary has no such relation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the status of the arbitrary.

parts.text: The arbitrary is neither true nor

feedback.note: That formula names an empty cognitive status, not a third kind of fact in reality.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about cognitive standing.

feedback.note: No standing means you do not park it on either side of a truth judgment.

exercises.prompt: Why is it a mistake to call the arbitrary false?

choices.text: False is a judgment, and a judgment needs a relation to evidence
Because calling something false is impolite
Because every unsupported claim later becomes true
Because only single words can be false

feedback.note: To judge a claim false you need grounds. An arbitrary string of words has not supplied any.

exercises.prompt: A friend invents a cause you have no reason to consider. What do you owe that story?

choices.text: Nothing: it is not yet a claim to accept or refute
A full proof that the story is impossible in every detail
Temporary belief until the story is tested
Agreement that it is probably true

feedback.note: Dismissal is not a positive theory of the opposite. It is a refusal to grant the story any cognitive role.

exercises.prompt: Fill the verb that names the right response.

parts.text: When a claim is arbitrary, you
it rather than weigh it as true or false.

feedback.note: Dismiss here means drop it from consideration, not insult the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Match the status to the example.

pairs.right: A story no evidence connects to anything
A report that contradicts what you perceive
A conclusion for which the evidence is sufficient

feedback.note: Keep the empty status separate from an actual falsehood and from a supported truth.

exercises.prompt: Build the caution about the opposite claim.

feedback.note: The opposite of an empty assertion is not automatically a piece of knowledge. It needs its own evidence.

lessons.title: Who must offer evidence
lessons.objective: Place the burden of proof on the person who asserts, and refuse the demand to disprove a claim that was never supported.

exercises.prompt: Who carries the burden of proof?

choices.text: The person who asserts the claim
Whoever hears the claim
Only someone who wants the claim to be false
No one; every claim stands until refuted

feedback.note: Asserting is what creates the need for evidence. Listening does not.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, You cannot prove my unsupported story is wrong, so you must accept it. What is wrong with that move?

choices.text: It shifts the burden onto the listener
The sentence is too long to be a claim
Listeners are required to be kind, and kindness is proof
Disproof is valid only if it arrives the same day

feedback.note: Failure to disprove an empty story is not evidence for the story. The asserter still owes the reasons.

exercises.prompt: Match each role to its job.

pairs.right: Must supply evidence if the claim is to be considered
May dismiss a claim that has no evidence
May take the claim up only after some evidence appears

feedback.note: Consideration starts when evidence shows up. Until then, no one else inherits a duty to refute.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule about burden.

parts.text: The burden of proof is on the person who

feedback.note: Hearing a claim, forgetting it, or doubting it does not move the burden onto you.

exercises.prompt: Build the reply to an empty demand for disproof.

feedback.note: You do not owe a refutation of what was never given a reason.

exercises.prompt: Evidence for a claim finally appears. What changes?

choices.text: The claim can now be examined as true or false
The claim is certain no matter how weak the evidence is
The claim was true the whole time it was arbitrary
Further questions become improper

feedback.note: Evidence lets the claim into cognition. It does not skip the work of judging how strong that evidence is.

exercises.prompt: Which demand is legitimate?

choices.text: Show the evidence for what you assert
Disprove every story I might invent
Accept my claim because I feel strongly
Believe it first and look for reasons later

feedback.note: Asking for evidence respects the burden. Demanding that others refute the unsupported does not.

exercises.prompt: Fill the word for what the listener need not do.

parts.text: a claim that still has no evidence.

feedback.note: Noticing that a claim is empty is enough. A refutation would treat it as a real alternative.

exercises.prompt: Match the move to the error or the proper step.

pairs.right: Illegitimate shift of the burden

pairs.left: Here is the observation that supports me
pairs.right: Proper acceptance of the burden

pairs.left: I will ignore your story until you offer a reason
pairs.right: Proper dismissal of the arbitrary

feedback.note: Offering a reason takes up the burden. Demanding agreement without one tries to dump it.

exercises.prompt: Build the order of proof.

feedback.note: Nothing cognitive is owed to a claim before evidence. Consideration follows the evidence.

lessons.title: Certainty inside a context
lessons.objective: Explain certainty as knowing that, inside a given context of evidence, nothing warrants doubt, without claiming to know every fact outside that context.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what is certainty?

choices.text: Recognizing a fact when the context of your knowledge gives no ground for doubt
Knowing every fact that will ever be discovered
A strong feeling with no need for evidence
Agreement by other people

feedback.note: Certainty is contextual. It is not omniscience, emotion, or a head count.

exercises.prompt: You see a cup on the desk and nothing in what you know suggests an illusion. What may you claim?

choices.text: Certainty that the cup is there, in this context
That no future discovery could ever add detail about the cup
Only that the cup is an arbitrary possibility
Knowledge of every cup that exists anywhere

feedback.note: The percept, with no contrary evidence in your context, is enough for certainty about this fact. It is not a claim to total knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.

pairs.right: The evidence and knowledge you actually have
No ground for doubt inside that evidence
Knowing everything, which certainty does not require

feedback.note: A context can grow. Certainty inside the present context is still certainty; it is not a guess.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of this kind of certainty.

parts.text: , not a claim to know every fact.

feedback.note: Contextual means judged against the knowledge you have, including the evidence that would be relevant to doubt.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that limits certainty without weakening it.

feedback.note: Later knowledge can add context. That possibility of growth is not a present ground for doubt.

exercises.prompt: When is doubt warranted?

choices.text: When some evidence in your context counts against the claim
Whenever you can say the words you might be wrong
Never, because certainty means the context can never grow
Whenever you feel uneasy, with or without a reason

feedback.note: Doubt is a cognitive response to contrary evidence, not a ritual phrase and not a mood.

exercises.prompt: New evidence later widens what you know about a fact you had been certain of. What follows?

choices.text: Your context grew; the earlier certainty still held for the context you had
The earlier certainty was never real
You must now treat every similar percept as arbitrary
You were omniscient and have now lost that status

feedback.note: Growth of knowledge does not erase a judgment that was fully supported in its context. It specifies or extends it.

exercises.prompt: Fill the condition that removes doubt.

parts.text: Inside a context, certainty means there is no evidence that warrants

feedback.note: If nothing in the context warrants doubt, the proper cognitive state is certainty, not a permanent maybe.

exercises.prompt: Match the situation to the verdict.

pairs.left: All available evidence agrees, and none conflicts
pairs.right: Contextually certain

pairs.left: Some evidence points the other way
pairs.right: Doubt is warranted

pairs.left: Someone says you might be wrong someday, with no evidence
pairs.right: Not a ground for doubt

feedback.note: Only evidence inside the context can open or close doubt. A bare someday does neither.

exercises.prompt: Build the summary of contextual certainty.

feedback.note: The phrase in this context keeps certainty tied to evidence without shrinking it into a guess.

lessons.title: Possibility is not a shrug
lessons.objective: Separate a genuine possibility, which some evidence supports, from an arbitrary maybe that cannot undercut contextual certainty.

exercises.prompt: When is something a genuine possibility?

choices.text: When some evidence supports it, even if the evidence is not yet conclusive
Whenever nobody has disproved it
Whenever someone can pronounce the word maybe
Whenever you would like it to be so

feedback.note: Possibility is a cognitive status. It requires some positive evidence, not a gap where a disproof has not been written.

exercises.prompt: You are certain, in context, that a book is on the shelf. A friend says, Maybe it is a hologram, and offers no evidence. What is that maybe?

choices.text: Arbitrary, so it does not undercut your certainty
A real possibility that forces you to suspend judgment
Proof that the senses never justify certainty
Equal in weight to seeing the book

feedback.note: An arbitrary maybe is not a possibility. It has no weight against evidence you already have.

exercises.prompt: Match each maybe to its status.

pairs.right: Rain is a genuine possibility

pairs.left: No evidence at all for a hidden cause
pairs.right: The hidden cause is arbitrary

pairs.left: Seeing the object, with nothing against it
pairs.right: Contextual certainty, not a mere maybe

feedback.note: Evidence can make a possibility, support a certainty, or be missing entirely. Those are three different standings.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

parts.text: A real possibility rests on some

feedback.note: Without some evidence, maybe does not name a possibility. It only repeats the arbitrary.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule that protects certainty.

feedback.note: Certainty yields to contrary evidence or to a supported alternative, not to a story with no basis.

exercises.prompt: Which slogan treats the arbitrary as if it were a possibility?

choices.text: Anything is possible, since nothing has been disproved in advance
Weigh the alternative that the measurements actually suggest
Trust the percept when no evidence contradicts it
Ask the asserter for a reason before you consider the claim

feedback.note: Anything is possible erases the difference between evidence and invention. The other lines keep that difference.

exercises.prompt: A laboratory result conflicts with a conclusion you had treated as certain. What should you do?

choices.text: Weigh the new evidence; this is a real challenge, not an arbitrary maybe
Ignore it, because certainty means the context is sealed forever
Drop all knowledge, because one result appeared
Call the result arbitrary even though it is evidence

feedback.note: Contrary evidence is a ground for reopening the context. That is different from a baseless maybe, which you dismiss.

exercises.prompt: Fill the status that some evidence creates.

parts.text: Some evidence, short of proof, makes a claim a

feedback.note: Possibility sits between dismissal and certainty. It still depends on evidence, and it is not yet proof.

exercises.prompt: Match the response to the input.

pairs.right: Dismiss it; certainty stands
Treat it as possible and keep checking

pairs.left: Evidence with no ground for doubt
pairs.right: Claim contextual certainty

feedback.note: The three responses match the three standings: arbitrary, possible, and certain.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing contrast of the unit.

feedback.note: Emptiness belongs to the unsupported claim. Certainty belongs to a fact that your present context of evidence fully supports.
